The cursor blinks. One thousand words. A simple instruction, almost a dare. I could write about anything: the smell of rain on asphalt, the way a stranger’s laugh can sound like a song you used to know, the quiet conspiracy of houseplants turning toward a window. But the blank page has a gravity of its own. It pulls the mind toward itself, and suddenly all the things I might have said dissolve into the white.

I think about word counts. They are strange creatures. They pretend to measure meaning, but they only measure length. A grocery list and a prayer can have the same number of words. A threat and a love letter. The Declaration of Independence is about 1,337 words. The Gettysburg Address is 272. Somewhere in between is the exact weight of a human heart, if you believe in metaphors. I don’t, but today I want to.

Outside, a dog is barking at something only it can see. The bark is sharp, then softer, then sharp again, like a question asked in a language I almost understand. I wonder if the dog is lonely or territorial. I wonder if I am projecting. The sky is the color of old pewter, and the trees are holding their breath before rain. If I were a better writer, I would make this moment mean something. Instead, I notice that my coffee has gone cold and that the word “pewter” feels heavy in my mouth.

When I was seven, I believed that words had physical weight. I thought “yes” was light and “no” was heavy, that “maybe” floated somewhere in between like a balloon that had lost most of its helium. I told my mother this, and she laughed, not unkindly, and said, “Then you should always say yes.” I tried. For a week, I said yes to everything: yes to extra broccoli, yes to a bath before dinner, yes to holding a spider. The spider was the end of it. Some words, I learned, are heavier than they look.

Now I am older, and I know that language is mostly shadow. We point at things and make sounds, and somehow we agree to call it truth. But there are moments when the shadow touches the thing itself. A friend says, “I’m tired,” and you feel the tiredness in your own bones. A song lyric lands on a wound you forgot you had. A stranger on a train looks at you with such kindness that you have to look away. Those are the moments I write for. Not the big declarations, but the small collisions.

I once read that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. I don’t know if that’s true. It sounds like too many. I imagine all those words drifting up from cities, from kitchens, from phones, from bedrooms, from arguments and apologies and bedtime stories. A cloud of language, thick enough to blot out the sun. What happens to the words we don’t mean? Do they fall back to earth as rain? Is that why some storms feel so sad?

My grandmother used to say, “Say what you mean, and mean what you say, but don’t say it mean.” She had a way of making the same word mean different things depending on how she tilted her head. “Come here” could be an invitation or a warning. “I love you” could be a fact or a plea. She died in October, when the leaves were doing their trick of pretending to be fire. At her funeral, I wanted to stand up and say something profound. Instead, I said, “She made the best cornbread.” Everyone laughed. It was true. Sometimes truth is small enough to fit in a cast-iron skillet.

I think about the 1000 words I have to write. I’ve used maybe 500 already. The number is not important. What matters is that I keep going, that I don’t stop at the first difficult sentence. Writing is just thinking with a deadline. You sit down, you open a vein, and you hope that what comes out is red and not gray. Some days it’s gray. Some days it’s a color you don’t have a name for, and you have to invent one.

If I could invent a word, it would mean “the feeling of almost remembering a dream.” I would use it in a sentence like: “She woke with a ______, the taste of someone’s name on her tongue.” I would use it until it became ordinary, until people forgot it was ever new. That’s what happens to all words. They start as magic and end as tools. Maybe that’s not a tragedy. Maybe it’s just how we build a life.

The rain has started. It taps on the window like a visitor who knows you’re not going to answer. The dog has stopped barking. The cursor blinks. I have 400 words left, give or take. I could write about the ocean. I could write about the first time I saw the ocean and thought, “This is too big to be real.” I could write about the way grief comes in waves, which is a cliché, but clichés are just truths that have been used too often because they work.

Instead, I’ll write about the sound of a page turning. It’s a small sound, almost nothing. But if you’re waiting for someone to finish reading something you wrote, it’s the loudest sound in the world. It means they’re still with you. It means they haven’t given up. It means the words are doing their job.

I don’t know who will read this. Maybe no one. Maybe you, at the end of a long day, looking for something to fill a quiet moment. If so, hello. I’m glad you’re here. I’m glad we could share these 1000 words, even though they’re just ink and electrons and a little bit of hope. The rain is falling. The dog is quiet. The cursor blinks. And somewhere, a page turns.

The cursor blinks. One thousand words. A simple instruction, almost a dare. I could write about anything: the smell of rain on asphalt, the way a stranger’s laugh can sound like a song you used to know, the quiet conspiracy of houseplants turning toward a window. But the blank page has a gravity of its own. It pulls the mind toward itself, and suddenly all the things I might have said dissolve into the white.

I think about word counts. They are strange creatures. They pretend to measure meaning, but they only measure length. A grocery list and a prayer can have the same number of words. A threat and a love letter. The Declaration of Independence is about 1,337 words. The Gettysburg Address is 272. Somewhere in between is the exact weight of a human heart, if you believe in metaphors. I don’t, always, but today I want to.

Outside, a dog is barking at something only it can see. The bark is sharp, then softer, then sharp again, like a question asked in a language I almost understand. I wonder if the dog is lonely or just territorial. I wonder if I am projecting. The sky is the color of old pewter, and the trees are holding their breath before rain. If I were a better writer, I would make this moment mean something. Instead, I notice that my coffee has gone cold and that the word “pewter” feels heavy in my mouth.

When I was seven, I believed that words had physical weight. I thought “yes” was light and “no” was heavy, that “maybe” floated somewhere in between like a balloon that had lost most of its helium. I told my mother this, and she laughed, not unkindly, and said, “Then you should always say yes.” I tried. For a week, I said yes to everything: yes to extra broccoli, yes to a bath before dinner, yes to holding a spider. The spider was the end of it. Some words, I learned, are heavier than they look.

Now I am older, and I know that language is mostly shadow. We point at things and make sounds, and somehow we agree to call it truth. But there are moments when the shadow touches the thing itself. A friend says, “I’m tired,” and you feel the tiredness in your own bones. A song lyric lands on a wound you forgot you had. A stranger on a train looks at you with such open kindness that you have to look away. Those are the moments I write for. Not the big declarations, but the small collisions.

I once read that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. I don’t know if that’s true. It sounds like too many. I imagine all those words drifting up from cities, from kitchens, from phones, from bedrooms, from arguments and apologies and bedtime stories. A cloud of language, thick enough to blot out the sun. What happens to the words we don’t mean? Do they fall back to earth as rain? Is that why some storms feel so sad?

My grandmother used to say, “Say what you mean, and mean what you say, but don’t say it mean.” She had a way of making the same word mean different things depending on how she tilted her head. “Come here” could be an invitation or a warning. “I love you” could be a fact or a plea. She died in October, when the leaves were doing their yearly trick of pretending to be fire. At her funeral, I wanted to stand up and say something profound. Instead, I said, “She made the best cornbread.” Everyone laughed. It was true. Sometimes truth is small enough to fit in a cast-iron skillet.

I think about the 1000 words I have to write. I’ve used maybe 500 already. The number is not important. What matters is that I keep going, that I don’t stop at the first difficult sentence. Writing is just thinking with a deadline. You sit down, you open a vein, and you hope that what comes out is red and not gray. Some days it’s gray. Some days it’s a color you don’t have a name for, and you have to invent one.

If I could invent a word, it would mean “the feeling of almost remembering a dream.” I would use it in a sentence like: “She woke with a ______, the taste of someone’s name on her tongue.” I would use it until it became ordinary, until people forgot it was ever new. That’s what happens to all words. They start as magic and end as tools. Maybe that’s not a tragedy. Maybe it’s just how we build a life.

The rain has started. It taps on the window like a polite visitor who knows you’re not going to answer. The dog has stopped barking. The cursor still blinks. I have 400 words left, give or take. I could write about the ocean. I could write about the first time I saw the ocean and thought, “This is too big to be real.” I could write about the way grief comes in waves, which is a cliché, but clichés are just truths that have been used too often because they work.

Instead, I’ll write about the sound of a page turning. It’s a small sound, almost nothing. But if you’re waiting for someone to finish reading something you wrote, it’s the loudest sound in the world. It means they’re still with you. It means they haven’t given up. It means the words are doing their job.

I don’t know who will read this. Maybe no one. Maybe you, right now, at the end of a long day, looking for something to fill a quiet moment. If so, hello. I’m glad you’re here. I’m glad we could share these 1000 words, even though they’re just ink and electrons and a little bit of hope. The rain is falling. The dog is quiet. The cursor blinks. And somewhere, a page turns.
